stem: Which two handlers should be throttled rather than debounced? (Choose two.)

options.text: Updating a reading-progress bar while the user keeps scrolling
options.why: The user wants steady updates during the scroll, at most every few frames.

options.text: Moving a dragged element while `mousemove` fires hundreds of times a second
options.why: Dragging must track the pointer continuously; throttling caps the work per second.

options.text: Sending a search request once the user stops typing
options.why: That waits for a pause, which is what debounce does.

options.text: Saving a draft after the user has stopped editing for two seconds
options.why: Again a pause-based trigger, so debounce is the right fit.

options.text: Recomputing a layout only after the window has finished resizing
options.why: Only the final size matters, so debounce avoids the wasted work.

explanation: Throttle runs at a steady maximum rate while events keep arriving; debounce waits for a quiet period and then runs once. Choose throttle when users need continuous feedback, and debounce when only the final state matters.

stem: A `once(fn)` helper, like lodash's `_.once`, should run `fn` on the first call only and return that first result on every later call.

options.text: False

explanation: A typical implementation: `let done = false, result; return function (...a) { if (!done) { done = true; result = fn.apply(this, a); } return result; }`. Setting `done` before calling `fn` also stops a re-entrant call from running it twice.

stem: Put the steps of the one-pass two-sum solution in order. It returns the indices of two numbers in `nums` that add up to `target`, in O(n) time.

If the map has `complement`, return `[map.get(complement), i]`
Otherwise store `n -> i` in the map and continue

explanation: Looking up the complement before storing the current number stops an element from pairing with itself (for `[3, 2, 4]` and target 6 it must not return `[0, 0]`). Each Map lookup and insert is O(1) on average, so the pass is O(n) time and O(n) space, against O(n²) for nested loops.

options.why: A mismatch, or an empty stack at that point, means the string is invalid.

options.text: Return true only if the stack is empty after the last character
options.why: Leftover openers, as in `"(("`, mean something was never closed.

options.text: Count the openers and closers of each kind, and accept when the counts are equal
options.why: Counts ignore order: `")("` and `"([)]"` have equal counts but are invalid.

options.text: Use `shift()` instead of `pop()`, so that the earliest opener is matched first
options.why: Brackets close last-in, first-out, so the most recent opener must match.

options.text: Sort the characters first, so that matching brackets end up next to each other

explanation: Push each opener; on each closer, pop and compare using a lookup such as `{ ')': '(', ']': '[', '}': '{' }`. Reject on a mismatch or an empty stack, and accept only if the stack ends empty. That is O(n) time and O(n) space.

`compose` applies functions right to left, like f(g(x)): `x * 2` gives 10, then `x + 1` gives 11. `pipe` is the left-to-right version (`reduce` instead of `reduceRight`), which would give (5 + 1) × 2 = 12.

options.why: A Map iterates in insertion order, so its first key is the one used longest ago.

options.why: The last key is the most recently used one, the opposite of what to evict.

explanation: A `Map` remembers insertion order, so re-inserting a key on every read moves it to the end. The first key is then always the least recently used, and eviction is O(1) with `keys().next().value`.

options.text: Entries expire at the next garbage collection, even while the node is still in the DOM
options.why: An entry lives as long as its key is reachable from somewhere else.

explanation: A WeakMap is the right cache for data derived per object (layout, parsed config, private state), because entries disappear along with their keys. The trade-offs: no iteration, no size, and object-only keys, so libraries pair a WeakMap for object arguments with a Map for primitives.
